In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between HBV status and the expression of ets2, IGF2, C-myc, N-ras and the occurrence of PHC.
the role of HBV in the carcinogenesis of PHCs.
the role of HBV and oncogenes in PHC and the possible mechanisms by which they contribute to PHC carcinogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the carcinogenesis of PHCs is a complex process, in which HBV plays a major role, but is not the sole cause.
HBV status is closely related to the carcinogenesis of PHCs, and the expression of ets2, IGFII, C-myc or N-ras is not a prerequisite to the development of PHCs.
HBV infection is an important factor in the carcinogenesis of PHCs, but the mechanism by which HBV causes PHC is not yet known.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PHC with free forms of defective HBV DNA is a special type of hepatocellular carcinoma.
the integrated and free forms of HBVs are both capable of inducing PHC.
the carcinogenesis of PHCs is a multi-stage, multi-factor process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HBV status, ets-2 expression, and IGF-II expression are related to the carcinogenesis of PHCs.
the carcinogenicity of HBV is not only due to its ability of integration into the host cell DNA.
the presence of free forms of HBsAg in PHC or adjacent nontumours may indicate the existence of defective HBsAg and the potential for carcinogenesis.
